That's because Kimi K3.1 Pro scores so high on third-party benchmarks — according to both Moonshot and [third-party AI model testing firm Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/kimi-k3-1-pro-launch-benchmarks) —it will almost certainly take the crown as the top open weights AI model in the world when Moonshot releases the weights under an open license, which the company says will happen a week and a half from now, on November 4, 2026. For now, developers and users can access it through its applications and developer [application programming interface (API)](https://platform.kimi.ai/?kssid=1731741809062039579), and its rates are half those of Claude Opus 5.5 and Meta’s Muse Wonder for input and output, although DeepSeek and Xiaomi remain cheaper. The facility, being developed by Nscale, was supposed to provide computing power for Microsoft's Azure cloud business. The problem? The electricity needed to run the data center wouldn't be available until the 2030s. Microsoft is maintaining its other agreements with Nscale, but the cancellation raises an important question about the enormous amounts of money being committed to AI infrastructure. What happens when a project doesn't work out? Companies make large commitments to build [AI](https://www.fool.com/terms/a/artificial-intelligence/) infrastructure. But there's a difference between selling the equipment needed to build an AI data center and owning that infrastructure while waiting for customers to pay for it. And that difference should matter to investors. ![Nvidia logo mounted on the exterior of a modern office building under a cloudy sky.](https://g.foolcdn.com/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fg.foolcdn.com%2Feditorial%2Fimages%2F890531%2Fnvidia_headquarters_exterior_nvidia_corporation_imagesource_getty_images_119.jpg&w=3840&op=resize) Image source: Nvidia. ## Three companies that get paid for hardware **Nvidia** ([NVDA](/quote/nasdaq/nvda/) -0.59%) is first on the list, and for good reason. Graphics processing units (GPUs) are considered must-have equipment for data centers, providing the computing power needed to train and operate advanced AI models. [Nvidia sells the processors and networking equipment](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/10/14/broadcom-vs-nvidia-if-i-could-only-own-one-for-the/). It generally recognizes revenue when the equipment is delivered under the applicable sales terms, rather than waiting years for the customer to earn a return. But Nvidia isn't completely insulated from its customers' financial problems. The company has invested in more than 200 other companies, many of them key tech, cloud, or infrastructure companies. highlights.content: **TRENDING:** * [Webinar | What It Takes to Make AI Trustworthy in Healthcare](/webinars/webinar-what-takes-to-make-ai-trustworthy-in-healthcare-w-7192?rf=TB)• * [2026 Resilience Week NYC: Healthcare, Fraud, & Finance Summits](https://ismg.events/general/resilience-week/?utm_source=trending)• [Agentic AI](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/agentic-ai-c-940) , [Identity Security](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/identity-security-c-607) # Matt Thompson Takes Transmit Helm as AI Agent Risks Grow Thompson Says Banks Must Move Beyond Blanket Blocks on Autonomous AI Agents [Michael Novinson](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/authors/michael-novinson-i-4923) ([MichaelNovinson](https://www.twitter.com/MichaelNovinson)) • October 19, 2026     * [Credit Eligible](/premium/pricing "As a BankInfoSecurity.com annual member, this content can be used toward your membership credits and transcript tracking.") ![Matt Thompson Takes Transmit Helm as AI Agent Risks Grow](https://ismg-cdn.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/articles/matt-thompson-takes-transmit-helm-as-ai-agent-risks-grow-image_large-4-a-33148.jpg) Matt Thompson, CEO, Transmit Security (Image: Transmit Security) Transmit Security selected Socure President Matt Thompson as its next CEO and tasked him with building infrastructure to manage autonomous artificial intelligence agent traffic. **See Also:** [Webinar | From Autonomy to Accountability: Securing the New Agentic Workforce](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/webinars/webinar-from-autonomy-to-accountability-securing-new-agentic-workforce-w-7388?rf=RAM_SeeAlso) The Tel Aviv, Israel, customer identity and access management provider wants Thompson to move it from a human identity orchestration to building foundational agent trust infrastructure. Thompson said Transmit will expand beyond its core base of large financial enterprises into the mid-market by streamlining implementation and adopting self-service models. "This is a time in the market where everyone is being hit by agents and needing to figure out, in a good way and in a bad way, how to manage that because allowing anything and blocking everything is just not going to be possible for businesses to continue to grow and protect their customers and their enterprises," Thompson told ISMG. Thompson spent more than five years at Socure, where he helped the Nevada identity and risk intelligence vendor grow the business by more than 500%. Transmit focuses on orchestrating identities across applications and managing authorization after login, while Socure focuses on onboarding, first-time identity verification, and validating identity-data changes (see: [*Socure Secures $156M, Buys Fravity to Automate Fraud Reviews*](/socure-secures-156m-buys-fravity-to-automate-fraud-reviews-a-32661)). ### Why Banks Can't Just Van Agents Thompson replaces Mickey Boodaei, who led the company since helping establish it in October 2014. He will remain involved as chairman of Transmit's board and involved day to day in implementing product strategy, while Thompson said he will take a larger role in shaping product strategy and setting priorities across the organization. "I see us providing foundational infrastructure for organizations to have visibility of what traffic is human traffic versus agent traffic," Thompson said. "That's kind of basic. Even as basic as it seems, it's a lot harder in practice." AI agents are actively executing tasks inside applications, and Thompson said the blanketed blocking policies in place at many financial institutions today are unsustainable long-term. Legitimate agent use cases are rapidly growing. AI agents are more iterative, adaptable, and persistent than humans, which Thompson said requires dedicated security controls and customized user journeys. "This isn't a tomorrow problem," Thompson said. "This is a yesterday problem for organizations to figure out, and a lot of them recognize they're behind. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Fine-Tune an LLM With QLoRA: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 25, 2026 · 35 min read You can fine-tune an LLM on a single consumer GPU in an afternoon, then run the result on your own machine through Ollama. The recipe is QLoRA: freeze a 4-bit copy of the base model, train small low-rank adapter matrices on top, merge the adapter, and export a GGUF file. The practical target here is a support-ticket triage model that returns strict JSON, trained on a synthetic dataset your own script generates in seconds. The [2023 QLoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314) from Tim Dettmers and coauthors made the core claim plainly: the method “reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.” Three years later the base models have changed, but the recipe has held up. What changed is the tooling around it, and that is where most readers get stuck. The stack moved fast this fall. Hugging Face’s latest TRL release is v1.16.0. PEFT v0.21.2 landed on October 1. Ollama v0.40.11 is the current release as of October 24. On the model side, Qwen3.8-27B, a dense, native vision-language model from Alibaba, is the newest 27B-class open-weight checkpoint covered here. If you only want inference on a big card, the walkthrough on [running LLMs locally on an RTX 5090](https://shattered.io/run-llm-locally-rtx-5090/) covers the serving half. What follows covers the training half, end to end. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Why Fine-Tune an LLM Instead of Prompting or RAG Most teams reach for fine-tuning too early. A good system prompt plus a few examples solves a large share of formatting problems, and retrieval-augmented generation handles anything that depends on fresh or private documents. So the first question is not how to fine tune LLM weights. It is whether you need to touch the weights at all. Fine-tuning earns its cost in four situations. The first is a rigid output format that the base model breaks even with careful prompting, such as strict JSON that a downstream parser consumes. The second is a narrow classification or extraction task where you have hundreds of labeled examples and want a small, cheap model to match a large one. The third is a house style or tone that a prompt cannot hold across thousands of calls. The fourth is latency and cost: a tuned model needs a short prompt, because the behavior lives in the weights instead of in 800 tokens of instructions you pay for on every request. It is the wrong tool for teaching a model new facts. Adapters shift behavior, and they absorb knowledge poorly and unreliably. If your goal is answering questions about a changing knowledge base, build retrieval and leave the weights alone. If you need both, tune for format and behavior, then add retrieval for facts. The two approaches stack cleanly. Open-weight models also make the economics different from two years ago. A ranking such as the one in the [best open source LLM roundup](https://shattered.io/best-open-source-llm-october-2026-kimi-glm-deepseek/) shows how many capable checkpoints now exist, and several of them ship under permissive licenses. That means you can tune, merge, and redistribute inside your company without negotiating an API contract. It also means you own the privacy story, since the training data never leaves your machine. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # TorchTPU Goes Open Source: 4 Repos, Oct. 20 [2026] ![Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/lbennett.webp) [Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/author/lbennett/) Updated Oct 26, 2026 · 16 min read Google and Meta open-sourced TorchTPU on October 20, 2026, giving PyTorch developers a native backend for Google TPUs. According to [Google Cloud’s announcement](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/torchtpu-is-now-open-source-run-native-pytorch-on-tpus), the project lets TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch. The reveal came at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 in San Jose, which ran October 20 to 21. The pitch is simple. Take a PyTorch workload you already run, point it at a TPU, and change as little code as you can. For years that promise sat behind a translation layer or a rewrite into another framework. TorchTPU tries to remove that tax, and it does so with Meta’s PyTorch team as a co-developer rather than a bystander. If you already serve models with vLLM, as in our [walkthrough for running an LLM on DGX Spark](https://shattered.io/run-llm-dgx-spark-ollama-vllm-12-steps-2026/), the new repositories suggest the same engine can now target a second kind of silicon. This analysis covers what shipped, what the sources confirm, what stays unproven, and what the release means for CUDA, JAX and the cloud accelerator market. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Google and Meta Announced at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 TorchTPU is an open-source collaboration between Google and Meta. It provides a native PyTorch backend for Google’s Tensor Processing Units. Google Cloud and InfoQ both report the announcement date as October 20, 2026, and the official event pages place the conference in San Jose, California. One naming detail deserves a correction. Many headlines say “PyTorch Conference 2026,” but the official event pages call it PyTorch Conference North America 2026. The distinction matters because the PyTorch community runs regional events, and a reader searching for session videos or slides needs the exact name. Two people introduced the project on stage. Bill Jia of Google Cloud and Zongwei Zhou, a Meta software engineer, presented TorchTPU alongside a segment on agentic developer workflows. The PyTorch project account announced the session on X, and the SGLang project posted its own note the same day saying it was officially open-sourcing TorchTPU for native, hardware-accelerated PyTorch execution on Cloud TPUs. The timeline also tells a story. Google started the effort in mid-2025 in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta. That means the project spent roughly a year or more in development before the public release, which is a normal runway for a compiler-heavy backend but a long one by the standards of AI tooling announcements. The release is not a product launch with a price tag. Nothing in the primary announcements gives a price, a benchmark or an adoption figure. What it gives is code, in the form of public repositories, and a clear statement of direction. That is the lens this article uses throughout. ## The Four Open-Source Repositories Behind TorchTPU Google and Meta did not ship a single library. They open-sourced four foundational repositories: TorchTPU, vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU and TorchTitan. Each covers a different layer of the stack, and together they map the path from a training run to a served model. TorchTPU is the core backend. It is the piece that lets PyTorch tensors and operations execute on a TPU as a first-class device. This development raises questions about the risks the company is assuming to support the global expansion of AI infrastructure. Having developed the chips that helped ignite the initial stages of the generative AI boom, Nvidia has leveraged its financial strength to fund AI model developers, data center operators, and a range of companies specializing in AI-focused cloud computing services. According to CNBC, the strategy employed by CEO Jensen Huang goes beyond simply developing cutting-edge technology; it involves investing in clients and assisting them in securing loans, thereby ensuring that Nvidia’s systems reach a broader user base. In this context, Nvidia capitalizes on its investment-grade credit rating by providing financial guarantees for large-scale projects—including those involving OpenAI—to help secure the funding necessary for infrastructure expansion at lower interest rates. According to the company’s latest quarterly financial disclosure in July, the value of off-balance-sheet AI cloud computing agreements—essentially financial guarantees provided by Nvidia to specialized cloud computing firms—reached approximately $36 billion. This is in addition to guarantees totaling up to $105 billion to cover costs for chips, land, and energy for a proposed OpenAI data center in the U.S. state of Ohio, which would have a capacity of up to 10 gigawatts. Nvidia has also entered into agreements to lease future data center capacity, valued at $20 billion, with the intention of transferring these contracts to third parties at a later date. In the vast majority of these agreements, Nvidia would only be required to make payments if the other parties involved in the projects fail to meet their obligations. David Trainer, founder and CEO of the financial research firm New Constructs, noted—as reported by CNBC—that if demand for computing capacity fails to grow at the exceptionally high levels anticipated, the market could face a significant problem. These risks emerge at a time when specialized cloud computing firms are facing mounting pressure in the financial markets. Shares in CoreWeave, Nebius, and Iris—all of which are backed by Nvidia and are currently incurring cash losses—each fell by at least 30% during the month of October. The cost of insuring against credit default for CoreWeave—the largest of these companies—has surged, with credit default swap (CDS) spreads exceeding 11%, as investors are forced to pay more to hedge against the risk of default. Other companies backed by Nvidia have also faced difficulties; for instance, the Australian AI cloud computing firm Firmus unexpectedly abandoned its plans for an initial public offering (IPO) in October. Meanwhile, the British company Enscale and SB Energy—which is backed by SoftBank—filed for IPOs in the United States in September, yet neither has provided any updates on their plans for several weeks. Nvidia shares ended Friday’s trading session lower for the third consecutive week on Wall Street, falling 7.6% in October—putting the stock on track for its worst monthly performance since November of last year. While AI systems have become increasingly capable of addressing individual clinical tasks, coordinating their outputs around the same patient remains a challenge. Tairex's approach is to move beyond standalone AI tools by developing an ecosystem of specialized agents that can work together within clinical workflows. Rather than building a single, all-purpose AI doctor, the company aims to enable AI systems to support physicians through coordinated, cross-specialty collaboration. **01. From Virtual Training to Real-World Collaboration** In a simulated environment populated by millions of highly realistic AI patients, an AI doctor can conduct tens of thousands of simulated consultations daily. These synthetic patients are partially generated based on clinical guidelines and medical literature rather than simply reproducing real medical records, helping mitigate patient privacy risks. This intensive virtual training yields a system comprising 54 AI doctors and millions of AI patients, covering more than 20 clinical specialties and tens of thousands of diseases. The AI doctors have achieved over 96% accuracy on the MedQA dataset. The system can learn from clinical feedback, adapting to doctors' consultation styles and diagnostic reasoning. The core capability of the newly launched Tairex Multidisciplinary Human-Agent Collaboration Ecosystem lies in its ability to organize specialized doctor avatar agents into a coordinated virtual team. When a patient's condition spans multiple specialties, the system dynamically activates relevant agents to work simultaneously. Rather than operating in silos, these agents present their clinical reasoning and evidence on a unified interface, with disagreements highlighted for the human physician's review. When an endocrinology agent proposed a beta-blocker for a patient with palpitations and a history of asthma, a respiratory medicine agent flagged that non-selective beta-blockers could trigger bronchoconstriction and suggested considering a selective beta-1 blocker. The case illustrates how collaboration among specialized AI agents can help doctors identify risks that may be overlooked from a single-specialty perspective. **02. AI Agents.content: **TRENDING:** * [Webinar | What It Takes to Make AI Trustworthy in Healthcare](/webinars/webinar-what-takes-to-make-ai-trustworthy-in-healthcare-w-7192?rf=TB)• * [2026 Resilience Week NYC: Healthcare, Fraud, & Finance Summits](https://ismg.events/general/resilience-week/?utm_source=trending)• [Agentic AI](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/agentic-ai-c-940) , [Identity Security](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/identity-security-c-607) # Matt Thompson Takes Transmit Helm as AI Agent Risks Grow Thompson Says Banks Must Move Beyond Blanket Blocks on Autonomous AI Agents [Michael Novinson](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/authors/michael-novinson-i-4923) ([MichaelNovinson](https://www.twitter.com/MichaelNovinson)) • October 19, 2026     * [Credit Eligible](/premium/pricing "As a BankInfoSecurity.com annual member, this content can be used toward your membership credits and transcript tracking.") ![Matt Thompson Takes Transmit Helm as AI Agent Risks Grow](https://ismg-cdn.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/articles/matt-thompson-takes-transmit-helm-as-ai-agent-risks-grow-image_large-4-a-33148.jpg) Matt Thompson, CEO, Transmit Security (Image: Transmit Security) Transmit Security selected Socure President Matt Thompson as its next CEO and tasked him with building infrastructure to manage autonomous artificial intelligence agent traffic. **See Also:** [Webinar | From Autonomy to Accountability: Securing the New Agentic Workforce](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/webinars/webinar-from-autonomy-to-accountability-securing-new-agentic-workforce-w-7388?rf=RAM_SeeAlso) The Tel Aviv, Israel, customer identity and access management provider wants Thompson to move it from a human identity orchestration to building foundational agent trust infrastructure. Thompson said Transmit will expand beyond its core base of large financial enterprises into the mid-market by streamlining implementation and adopting self-service models. "This is a time in the market where everyone is being hit by agents and needing to figure out, in a good way and in a bad way, how to manage that because allowing anything and blocking everything is just not going to be possible for businesses to continue to grow and protect their customers and their enterprises," Thompson told ISMG. Thompson spent more than five years at Socure, where he helped the Nevada identity and risk intelligence vendor grow the business by more than 500%. Transmit focuses on orchestrating identities across applications and managing authorization after login, while Socure focuses on onboarding, first-time identity verification, and validating identity-data changes (see: [*Socure Secures $156M, Buys Fravity to Automate Fraud Reviews*](/socure-secures-156m-buys-fravity-to-automate-fraud-reviews-a-32661)). ### Why Banks Can't Just Van Agents Thompson replaces Mickey Boodaei, who led the company since helping establish it in October 2014. He will remain involved as chairman of Transmit's board and involved day to day in implementing product strategy, while Thompson said he will take a larger role in shaping product strategy and setting priorities across the organization. "I see us providing foundational infrastructure for organizations to have visibility of what traffic is human traffic versus agent traffic," Thompson said. "That's kind of basic. Even as basic as it seems, it's a lot harder in practice." AI agents are actively executing tasks inside applications, and Thompson said the blanketed blocking policies in place at many financial institutions today are unsustainable long-term. Legitimate agent use cases are rapidly growing. AI agents are more iterative, adaptable, and persistent than humans, which Thompson said requires dedicated security controls and customized user journeys. "This isn't a tomorrow problem," Thompson said. "This is a yesterday problem for organizations to figure out, and a lot of them recognize they're behind. While AI systems have become increasingly capable of addressing individual clinical tasks, coordinating their outputs around the same patient remains a challenge. Tairex's approach is to move beyond standalone AI tools by developing an ecosystem of specialized agents that can work together within clinical workflows. Rather than building a single, all-purpose AI doctor, the company aims to enable AI systems to support physicians through coordinated, cross-specialty collaboration. **01. From Virtual Training to Real-World Collaboration** In a simulated environment populated by millions of highly realistic AI patients, an AI doctor can conduct tens of thousands of simulated consultations daily. These synthetic patients are partially generated based on clinical guidelines and medical literature rather than simply reproducing real medical records, helping mitigate patient privacy risks. This intensive virtual training yields a system comprising 54 AI doctors and millions of AI patients, covering more than 20 clinical specialties and tens of thousands of diseases. The AI doctors have achieved over 96% accuracy on the MedQA dataset. The system can learn from clinical feedback, adapting to doctors' consultation styles and diagnostic reasoning. The core capability of the newly launched Tairex Multidisciplinary Human-Agent Collaboration Ecosystem lies in its ability to organize specialized doctor avatar agents into a coordinated virtual team. When a patient's condition spans multiple specialties, the system dynamically activates relevant agents to work simultaneously. Rather than operating in silos, these agents present their clinical reasoning and evidence on a unified interface, with disagreements highlighted for the human physician's review. When an endocrinology agent proposed a beta-blocker for a patient with palpitations and a history of asthma, a respiratory medicine agent flagged that non-selective beta-blockers could trigger bronchoconstriction and suggested considering a selective beta-1 blocker. The case illustrates how collaboration among specialized AI agents can help doctors identify risks that may be overlooked from a single-specialty perspective. **02. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # TorchTPU Goes Open Source: 4 Repos, Oct. 20 [2026] ![Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/lbennett.webp) [Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/author/lbennett/) Updated Oct 26, 2026 · 16 min read Google and Meta open-sourced TorchTPU on October 20, 2026, giving PyTorch developers a native backend for Google TPUs. According to [Google Cloud’s announcement](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/torchtpu-is-now-open-source-run-native-pytorch-on-tpus), the project lets TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch. The reveal came at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 in San Jose, which ran October 20 to 21. The pitch is simple. Take a PyTorch workload you already run, point it at a TPU, and change as little code as you can. For years that promise sat behind a translation layer or a rewrite into another framework. TorchTPU tries to remove that tax, and it does so with Meta’s PyTorch team as a co-developer rather than a bystander. If you already serve models with vLLM, as in our [walkthrough for running an LLM on DGX Spark](https://shattered.io/run-llm-dgx-spark-ollama-vllm-12-steps-2026/), the new repositories suggest the same engine can now target a second kind of silicon. This analysis covers what shipped, what the sources confirm, what stays unproven, and what the release means for CUDA, JAX and the cloud accelerator market. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Google and Meta Announced at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 TorchTPU is an open-source collaboration between Google and Meta. It provides a native PyTorch backend for Google’s Tensor Processing Units. Google Cloud and InfoQ both report the announcement date as October 20, 2026, and the official event pages place the conference in San Jose, California. One naming detail deserves a correction. Many headlines say “PyTorch Conference 2026,” but the official event pages call it PyTorch Conference North America 2026. The distinction matters because the PyTorch community runs regional events, and a reader searching for session videos or slides needs the exact name. Two people introduced the project on stage. Bill Jia of Google Cloud and Zongwei Zhou, a Meta software engineer, presented TorchTPU alongside a segment on agentic developer workflows. The PyTorch project account announced the session on X, and the SGLang project posted its own note the same day saying it was officially open-sourcing TorchTPU for native, hardware-accelerated PyTorch execution on Cloud TPUs. The timeline also tells a story. Google started the effort in mid-2025 in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta. That means the project spent roughly a year or more in development before the public release, which is a normal runway for a compiler-heavy backend but a long one by the standards of AI tooling announcements. The release is not a product launch with a price tag. Nothing in the primary announcements gives a price, a benchmark or an adoption figure. What it gives is code, in the form of public repositories, and a clear statement of direction. That is the lens this article uses throughout. ## The Four Open-Source Repositories Behind TorchTPU Google and Meta did not ship a single library. They open-sourced four foundational repositories: TorchTPU, vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU and TorchTitan. Each covers a different layer of the stack, and together they map the path from a training run to a served model. TorchTPU is the core backend. It is the piece that lets PyTorch tensors and operations execute on a TPU as a first-class device. The other three repositories sit on top of it or beside it. vLLM-TorchTPU and SGLang-TorchTPU target inference...

LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Fine-Tune an LLM With QLoRA: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 25, 2026 · 35 min read You can fine-tune an LLM on a single consumer GPU in an afternoon, then run the result on your own machine through Ollama. The recipe is QLoRA: freeze a 4-bit copy of the base model, train small low-rank adapter matrices on top, merge the adapter, and export a GGUF file. The practical target here is a support-ticket triage model that returns strict JSON, trained on a synthetic dataset your own script generates in seconds. The [2023 QLoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314) from Tim Dettmers and coauthors made the core claim plainly: the method “reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.” Three years later the base models have changed, but the recipe has held up. What changed is the tooling around it, and that is where most readers get stuck. The stack moved fast this fall. Hugging Face’s latest TRL release is v1.16.0. PEFT v0.21.2 landed on October 1. Ollama v0.40.11 is the current release as of October 24. On the model side, Qwen3.8-27B, a dense, native vision-language model from Alibaba, is the newest 27B-class open-weight checkpoint covered here. If you only want inference on a big card, the walkthrough on [running LLMs locally on an RTX 5090](https://shattered.io/run-llm-locally-rtx-5090/) covers the serving half. What follows covers the training half, end to end. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Why Fine-Tune an LLM Instead of Prompting or RAG Most teams reach for fine-tuning too early. A good system prompt plus a few examples solves a large share of formatting problems, and retrieval-augmented generation handles anything that depends on fresh or private documents. So the first question is not how to fine tune LLM weights. It is whether you need to touch the weights at all. Fine-tuning earns its cost in four situations. The first is a rigid output format that the base model breaks even with careful prompting, such as strict JSON that a downstream parser consumes. The second is a narrow classification or extraction task where you have hundreds of labeled examples and want a small, cheap model to match a large one. The third is a house style or tone that a prompt cannot hold across thousands of calls. The fourth is latency and cost: a tuned model needs a short prompt, because the behavior lives in the weights instead of in 800 tokens of instructions you pay for on every request. It is the wrong tool for teaching a model new facts. Adapters shift behavior, and they absorb knowledge poorly and unreliably. LLMs.titleZh: AI-generated text is growing harder to understand, study finds | LavX News
LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![AI-generated text is growing harder to understand, study finds](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fai-generated-text-is-growing-harder-to-understand-study-finds-1_1792918142277-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #LLMs # AI-generated text is growing harder to understand, study finds • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •1 min read Share this article Researchers analyzed psycholinguistic features across nine frontier AI models and found AI text packs in more complex syntax and rare phrases than human writing. They argue optimization for reasoning and code—not conversation—is driving the shift. A study posted to arXiv on Oct. 21 suggests AI-generated language is growing harder for humans to parse, and the cause is a shift in optimization targets rather than sloppy training. Thomas Clark, Matias Martin and Kyle Mahowald built a novel corpus of AI text across domains and measured features tied to human processing difficulty: object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies and low-frequency n-grams. The nine frontier and near-frontier models they tested used these features at higher rates than paraphrases from round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine deployed more inanimate subjects paired with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams. Many used longer dependencies, stacked nouns and reduced object relatives in conversation. The researchers noted wide variation across model families. The team proposes a cause. Human language evolved for successful communication. Developers now optimize LLMs for math, code and reasoning, which demands high information density. That demand pushes models toward compressed syntax over clarity. To test this, they fine-tuned a language model under a length penalty. The model diverged from human-like linguistic patterns, supporting the idea that compression drives the change. The findings highlight a misalignment: what makes text efficient for reasoning often makes it harder for human readers. The authors point toward remedies that could rebalance these goals. The paper is available at [arXiv:2610.29162](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.29162). LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Adaptive Temperature Distillation Shrinks Multilingual AI Models for Classroom Use ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Adaptive Temperature Distillation Shrinks Multilingual AI Models for Classroom Use](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-14995-750x422.png) Adaptive Temperature Distillation Shrinks Multilingual AI Models for Classroom Use A team of researchers reports in Discover Artificial Intelligence that a new compression framework can shrink a large multilingual language model into a lightweight student that keeps nearly all of the teacher’s performance across more than forty languages. The method, called adaptive temperature distillation with curriculum learning, distills the 560-million-parameter XLM-RoBERTa-Large model into a student with only 66 million parameters, about 11.8 percent of the original size. The compressed model reaches an average accuracy of 84.1 percent across five multilingual benchmarks, corresponding to 97.8 percent of the teacher’s performance, while running inference 8.5 times faster and fitting into roughly 260 megabytes of memory instead of the teacher’s 2.2 gigabytes. Compared with standard knowledge distillation, the framework improves overall accuracy by 4.6 percentage points, and the gains are largest precisely where compression usually hurts most: languages with little training data. The motivation comes from education, where large multilingual models promise personalized tutoring, automated feedback and instructional support in students’ native languages, but remain impractical to deploy. The authors note that more than 1.6 billion students worldwide have used online learning platforms, creating demand for smart educational assistants in many languages and cultures. Yet models of XLM-RoBERTa-Large’s scale require gigabytes of memory and high-performance GPU hardware, with inference latencies typically in the hundreds of milliseconds. An interactive intelligent tutoring system needs responses in under 100 milliseconds to keep students engaged, and cloud-based inference carries high operating costs and energy consumption. These constraints are especially severe in low-resource regions with unreliable internet connections and limited computing facilities, which the researchers argue are exactly the places where multilingual educational support is needed most urgently. Standard knowledge distillation, in which a small student model is trained to mimic the output distribution of a large teacher, runs into a fundamental problem in multilingual settings: it uses a single fixed temperature parameter for every language and every sample. The temperature controls how sharply the teacher’s probability distribution is softened before the student learns from it, exposing what distillation researchers call dark knowledge, the relative probabilities of incorrect classes that reveal how classes relate to one another. According to evidence cited in the paper, applying standard distillation to multilingual models causes performance drops of roughly 20 to 30 percent overall, with low-resource languages falling by as much as 40 percent. High-resource languages such as English and Chinese, rich in training data, learn differently from low-resource languages such as Swahili and Urdu, and no single temperature value can serve both regimes at once. Existing methods also treat all training samples uniformly, exposing the student to complex examples before it has built solid basic representations. The first component of the new framework is a learnable temperature predictor that dynamically adjusts the softmax temperature for each sample. The motivation comes from education, where large multilingual models promise personalized tutoring, automated feedback and instructional support in students’ native languages, but remain impractical to deploy. Open Source AI.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Fine-Tune an LLM With QLoRA: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 25, 2026 · 35 min read You can fine-tune an LLM on a single consumer GPU in an afternoon, then run the result on your own machine through Ollama. The recipe is QLoRA: freeze a 4-bit copy of the base model, train small low-rank adapter matrices on top, merge the adapter, and export a GGUF file. The practical target here is a support-ticket triage model that returns strict JSON, trained on a synthetic dataset your own script generates in seconds. The [2023 QLoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314) from Tim Dettmers and coauthors made the core claim plainly: the method “reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.” Three years later the base models have changed, but the recipe has held up. What changed is the tooling around it, and that is where most readers get stuck. The stack moved fast this fall. Hugging Face’s latest TRL release is v1.16.0. PEFT v0.21.2 landed on October 1. Ollama v0.40.11 is the current release as of October 24. On the model side, Qwen3.8-27B, a dense, native vision-language model from Alibaba, is the newest 27B-class open-weight checkpoint covered here. If you only want inference on a big card, the walkthrough on [running LLMs locally on an RTX 5090](https://shattered.io/run-llm-locally-rtx-5090/) covers the serving half. What follows covers the training half, end to end. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Why Fine-Tune an LLM Instead of Prompting or RAG Most teams reach for fine-tuning too early. A good system prompt plus a few examples solves a large share of formatting problems, and retrieval-augmented generation handles anything that depends on fresh or private documents. So the first question is not how to fine tune LLM weights. It is whether you need to touch the weights at all. Fine-tuning earns its cost in four situations. The first is a rigid output format that the base model breaks even with careful prompting, such as strict JSON that a downstream parser consumes. The second is a narrow classification or extraction task where you have hundreds of labeled examples and want a small, cheap model to match a large one. The third is a house style or tone that a prompt cannot hold across thousands of calls. The fourth is latency and cost: a tuned model needs a short prompt, because the behavior lives in the weights instead of in 800 tokens of instructions you pay for on every request. It is the wrong tool for teaching a model new facts. Adapters shift behavior, and they absorb knowledge poorly and unreliably. If your goal is answering questions about a changing knowledge base, build retrieval and leave the weights alone. If you need both, tune for format and behavior, then add retrieval for facts. The two approaches stack cleanly. Open-weight models also make the economics different from two years ago. A ranking such as the one in the [best open source LLM roundup](https://shattered.io/best-open-source-llm-october-2026-kimi-glm-deepseek/) shows how many capable checkpoints now exist, and several of them ship under permissive licenses. That means you can tune, merge, and redistribute inside your company without negotiating an API contract. It also means you own the privacy story, since the training data never leaves your machine. MiniMax's technology export registration covers some recently released and soon-to-be-released models, spanning both open-source release and overseas licensing. The move follows the October 16 public consultation by China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology on a revision to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, which proposes adding 23 AI technologies to export controls. Industry insiders say the overseas path for general-purpose open-source LLMs is thus becoming clearer, overseas customers' wait-and-see stance on the compliance risks of Chinese models is expected to ease, and small and mid-sized vendors now have a compliance template to follow. ##### Key Elements ![DeepSeek, MiniMax Complete Registration for LLM Overseas Expansion as Compliance Channel for Open-Source Models Takes Shape](https://img.biggo.com/_Civ6fNOD09dTgxLFBGElEhWP0sWCqtffoasYcZTMV4/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzZkZjhhZjI2LTQzNTEtNDIxOS04ZGE5LTUxYjAyYTgzODIyN18xNzkyOTUzMTgxX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) The overseas expansion of China's domestic artificial intelligence large language models has made substantive progress. According to a report on October 23 by Yuyuantantian, a new media outlet under China Central Television, DeepSeek and MiniMax have completed the relevant registration procedures and cleared the compliance process for the open-source release and overseas licensing of their large language models. This means that while core sensitive technologies remain strictly controlled, the overseas path for general-purpose open-source LLMs is instead becoming clearer. According to Science and Technology Innovation Board Daily, MiniMax's technology export registration covers "some recently released and soon-to-be-released models," spanning the two core scenarios of open-source release and overseas licensing. In other words, the company's registration is not a one-off filing for a single model but reserves compliance room for its subsequent model iterations. The direct backdrop to this progress is the October 16 joint announcement by China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology opening a public consultation on a revision to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. Open Source AI.titleZh: Hi3D V1.0: AI Generator for Printable 3D Models Now Available as Open Source
Open Source AI.content: ![3Druck.com - The Independent AM Magazine](https://3druck.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3Druck-Logo-2026.png) #### Industries #### Business #### Technology # Hi3D V1.0: AI Generator for Printable 3D Models Now Available as Open Source ![](https://3druck.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/hi3d-v1.jpg "hi3d-v1") **[Hi3D](https://www.hi3d.ai/) has released its AI model, Hi3D V1.0, as open source. The model generates high-resolution 3D geometry and was previously known as Sparc3D. The company has made the source code available on [GitHub](https://github.com/hi3d-official/Hi3Dv1.0), and the model weights on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/hi3d-official/Hi3Dv1.0). There is also a [demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ilcve21/Sparc3D). You can also create models for free on the Hi3D website. According to Hi3D, 90 percent of the models created can be successfully sliced.** Sparc3D stood out in 2025 for its highly detailed geometry. Since then, the team has expanded the training data from approximately 500,000 to about two million selected 3D objects. It also tested the model in real production processes. The step-by-step reconstruction of the geometry now achieves an effective sparse-grid resolution of up to 1536³. Fine structures are to be preserved, and the shape is to be consistent across multiple viewpoints. According to the manufacturer, the model achieved the best results in terms of detail and accuracy across multiple views in the company’s own evaluation. The announcement does not specify which models Hi3D used for comparison. In addition to 3D printing, Hi3D lists e-commerce and industrial design among its areas of application, [VR](https://3druck.com/en/glossary/vr/)- as well as AR applications, animation, and film. Companies and developers can run the model on their own servers, integrate it into existing workflows, and build their own services on top of it. However, this is only permitted within the scope of the respective license. The announcement does not specify which license this is. **3Druck.com** Set as the preferred source on Google The open model belongs to an older generation. Hi3D already offers Version 3.0 commercially, which works with 2048³ voxels and, according to the company, delivers finer details and better textures. The platform also provides two tools for print preparation. One breaks models down into printable parts and adds connectors for assembly. Another converts textured models into color regions for multicolor printing. In addition, there is the Hi3D Agent, which links language models to the user’s own 3D model, and an MCP interface for external applications. Open Source AI.content: [![TOKENPOST](/tokenpost-logo.svg)](/) 2 min read [![](/google-g.png)Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=tokenpost.com) # LiteLLM Traces Malicious Release to Master Key Left Unrevoked The key was exposed in May. LiteLLM’s timeline links it to stolen GitHub access and a redirected release pipeline in October. ![](https://f1.tokenpost.com/2024/11/9vga9k0r6d.png) By **[Simon Yoon](/reporters/26)** Published ![A red-highlighted file row stands out on a laptop screen / TokenPost.ai](https://mzwrodgsdjfdyvnraeya.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/article-media/articles/407a37824b2d3f3817806f6697ee3662a8247b8df4c2a95dc13d023e65c8bf8d.webp) A red-highlighted file row stands out on a laptop screen / TokenPost.ai LiteLLM traced its malicious v1.107.0 release to an Agent Platform master key committed to a public repository in May and left active, linking the Oct. 21 compromise to a credential exposure that began months earlier. LiteLLM’s open-source gateway lets applications connect to more than 100 large language model providers through a single interface. The new root-cause timeline adds to [earlier coverage of the release’s credential risks and remediation](https://www.tokenpost.com/news/technology/38009), detailing how the incident reached the release pipeline. A configuration file containing the master key was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository May 27. The key had been flagged for revocation but remained active. On Oct. 10 at 5:27:10 p.m. ET (21:27:10 UTC), an API response returned a GitHub CLI OAuth token associated with an organization owner. LiteLLM’s investigation traces the attacker’s subsequent use of CI workflows to obtain tokens for two maintainers. On Oct. 21, the owner’s token was used to override branch protections and redirect the release workflow from BerriAI/litellm to the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm repository. A maintainer’s token approved the production release. Release controls had been relaxed to let two engineers trigger and approve more frequent bug-fix releases. Seven malicious PyPI wheels were published between 7:39:51 and 7:40:13 a.m. ET (11:39:51–11:40:13 UTC). The package was removed by 9:23 a.m. ET (13:23 UTC). Docker Hub and GitHub Container Registry images were published at 7:46:56 a.m. ET (11:46:56 UTC). Affected GitHub Container Registry tags were unavailable by 9:51 a.m. ET (13:51 UTC), while Docker Hub tags were removed or pointed to clean images by 10:20 a.m. ET (14:20 UTC). LiteLLM identified litellm==1.107.0 and Docker tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest and main-stable as affected. The payload stole credentials and loaded tools for remote code execution. LiteLLM’s private enterprise release was not affected. The company planned to share process improvements during the week of Oct. 26. ![](https://f1.tokenpost.com/2024/11/9vga9k0r6d.png) ## Simon Yoon Reporter Simon Yoon reports on blockchain technology for TokenPost. The facility, being developed by Nscale, was supposed to provide computing power for Microsoft's Azure cloud business. The problem? The electricity needed to run the data center wouldn't be available until the 2030s. Microsoft is maintaining its other agreements with Nscale, but the cancellation raises an important question about the enormous amounts of money being committed to AI infrastructure. What happens when a project doesn't work out? Companies make large commitments to build [AI](https://www.fool.com/terms/a/artificial-intelligence/) infrastructure. But there's a difference between selling the equipment needed to build an AI data center and owning that infrastructure while waiting for customers to pay for it. And that difference should matter to investors. ![Nvidia logo mounted on the exterior of a modern office building under a cloudy sky.](https://g.foolcdn.com/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fg.foolcdn.com%2Feditorial%2Fimages%2F890531%2Fnvidia_headquarters_exterior_nvidia_corporation_imagesource_getty_images_119.jpg&w=3840&op=resize) Image source: Nvidia. ## Three companies that get paid for hardware **Nvidia** ([NVDA](/quote/nasdaq/nvda/) -0.59%) is first on the list, and for good reason. Graphics processing units (GPUs) are considered must-have equipment for data centers, providing the computing power needed to train and operate advanced AI models. [Nvidia sells the processors and networking equipment](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/10/14/broadcom-vs-nvidia-if-i-could-only-own-one-for-the/). It generally recognizes revenue when the equipment is delivered under the applicable sales terms, rather than waiting years for the customer to earn a return. But Nvidia isn't completely insulated from its customers' financial problems. The company has invested in more than 200 other companies, many of them key tech, cloud, or infrastructure companies. Infra & Chips.content: Sunday 25 October ,2026 [![Maaal News](/_next/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fstage.maaal.com%2Fstorage%2Fuploads%2Fphotos%2Fsettings%2F2026-10%2F1879658022848158.webp&w=256&q=75)](/en/) [![Maaal News](/_next/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fstage.maaal.com%2Fstorage%2Fuploads%2Fphotos%2Fsettings%2F2026-10%2F1879658022848158.webp&w=256&q=75)](/en/) * [Home](/en/) * [Articles](/en/articles/) * [Maaal Authors](/en/authors/) * [العربية](/ar/news/details/cloud-computing-sector-do/) [English](/en/news/details/cloud-computing-sector-do/) # Cloud Computing Sector Downturn Puts Nvidia’s AI-Boom Financing Bets to the Test Maaal: «Riyadh»Published: 25 October 2026 Share through Share through 16 Nvidia is facing a stern test of its financing strategy for the artificial intelligence sector, as credit markets tighten lending conditions for several of its key partners. This development raises questions about the risks the company is assuming to support the global expansion of AI infrastructure. Having developed the chips that helped ignite the initial stages of the generative AI boom, Nvidia has leveraged its financial strength to fund AI model developers, data center operators, and a range of companies specializing in AI-focused cloud computing services. According to CNBC, the strategy employed by CEO Jensen Huang goes beyond simply developing cutting-edge technology; it involves investing in clients and assisting them in securing loans, thereby ensuring that Nvidia’s systems reach a broader user base. In this context, Nvidia capitalizes on its investment-grade credit rating by providing financial guarantees for large-scale projects—including those involving OpenAI—to help secure the funding necessary for infrastructure expansion at lower interest rates. According to the company’s latest quarterly financial disclosure in July, the value of off-balance-sheet AI cloud computing agreements—essentially financial guarantees provided by Nvidia to specialized cloud computing firms—reached approximately $36 billion. This is in addition to guarantees totaling up to $105 billion to cover costs for chips, land, and energy for a proposed OpenAI data center in the U.S. state of Ohio, which would have a capacity of up to 10 gigawatts. Nvidia has also entered into agreements to lease future data center capacity, valued at $20 billion, with the intention of transferring these contracts to third parties at a later date. In the vast majority of these agreements, Nvidia would only be required to make payments if the other parties involved in the projects fail to meet their obligations. David Trainer, founder and CEO of the financial research firm New Constructs, noted—as reported by CNBC—that if demand for computing capacity fails to grow at the exceptionally high levels anticipated, the market could face a significant problem. These risks emerge at a time when specialized cloud computing firms are facing mounting pressure in the financial markets. Shares in CoreWeave, Nebius, and Iris—all of which are backed by Nvidia and are currently incurring cash losses—each fell by at least 30% during the month of October. The cost of insuring against credit default for CoreWeave—the largest of these companies—has surged, with credit default swap (CDS) spreads exceeding 11%, as investors are forced to pay more to hedge against the risk of default. Other companies backed by Nvidia have also faced difficulties; for instance, the Australian AI cloud computing firm Firmus unexpectedly abandoned its plans for an initial public offering (IPO) in October. Meanwhile, the British company Enscale and SB Energy—which is backed by SoftBank—filed for IPOs in the United States in September, yet neither has provided any updates on their plans for several weeks. The conversation ranges across the energy build-out, why he thinks hardware captures the margin in the stack, the shift from producing AI output to verifying it, and why he expects robotics to dwarf agentic coding; the $10 trillion inference forecast in the title is one line inside a much broader discussion of compute architecture, data curation, and investing. Rao sold Mosaic ML to Databricks for $1.3 billion and now runs Unconventional AI, which he describes as building a computer designed around energy efficiency rather than speed; he says its last round closed at close to a $5 billion valuation. He speaks as both a chip designer and an active seed investor, which lets him move between silicon physics, model training curricula, and venture pricing in the same conversation. The reader should come away with his specific numbers on power and compute, his framework for where margin sits in the AI stack, and his view that the current market wobble is a blip rather than a bubble. ## Energy is the binding constraint, and the spare capacity runs out within a few years Rao's central claim is that the AI build-out is consuming a finite pool of excess grid capacity, and that once it is gone the industry converges to the much slower rate at which power plants can actually be built. He puts the cost of one gigawatt at roughly $50 billion, more than the $20–30 billion cost of a semiconductor fab, and says people throw the word "gigawatt" around without appreciating that complexity. The U.S. grid averages about 900 gigawatts of output but can peak at roughly 1.2–1.3 terawatts, and the last several years of data-center growth have come mainly from running that existing infrastructure at higher utilization rather than from new construction. His timeline is short. Even on conservative AI growth assumptions, he says, "we're going to be out of energy pretty soon in the next few years." He is openly skeptical of announced build rates: "I've heard people say, oh, we're going to build 40 gigawatts in a year. There's no way. We have never done that." Ten gigawatts in a year would be an achievement, and at $50 billion per gigawatt that is half a trillion dollars of construction. On China, Rao credits central planning as a genuine advantage for large infrastructure rollouts — China surpassed the U.S. in total capacity around 2023 after building roughly six times faster for two decades, much of it coal — while arguing the U.S. retains the edge at "the tip of the spear" of innovation, noting AI was born in the U.S. and that Chinese labs are now doing real innovation rather than only distillation. He sees a two-tier electricity market already forming. Behind-the-meter deals are bespoke and priced well above standard grid rates, which he says makes sense because a gigawatt of compute can be sold for something like five times the cost of the electricity that powers it, leaving room to pay 30–40% more per kilowatt-hour. Infra & Chips.content: [## the tech buzz](/) SpaceX Secures $40 Billion Debt Financing for AI Chip Infrastructure [AI](/topics/ai)/[SpaceX](/topics/spacex) # SpaceX Secures $40 Billion Debt Financing for AI Chip Infrastructure SpaceX has closed a massive $40 billion debt deal to purchase GPUs for AI infrastructure, according to CEO Elon Musk, marking one of the largest technology infrastructure investments in recent history. by [The Tech Buzz](/authors/the-tech-buzz) PUBLISHED: Mon, Oct 26, 2026, 1:06 AM UTC| UPDATED: Mon, Oct 26, 2026, 1:06 AM UTC [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) ![Server rack containing stacked graphics processing units with cooling systems and cables in a data center.](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,quality=85,format=auto,fit=cover/https://charming-card-d91ad3487b.media.strapiapp.com/large_spacex_secures_40_billion_debt_financing_for_ai_chip_infrastructure_8a4565a6ba.jpg) Photo: Server rack containing stacked graphics processing units with cooling systems and cables in a data center. AI-generated illustration by The Tech Buzz. Edited by Barnabas Oretan (The Tech Buzz).· AI-generated image In a significant move that underscores the growing importance of AI infrastructure, SpaceX has successfully closed $40 billion in debt financing dedicated to purchasing graphics processing units (GPUs), CEO Elon Musk announced. This unprecedented investment highlights the aerospace company's expansion into AI computing capabilities and represents one of the largest single infrastructure investments in the technology sector. The $40 billion debt financing package represents a remarkable commitment to AI infrastructure at a scale rarely seen in the technology industry. While specific details about the lenders, terms, and timeline of the deal remain limited based on available information, the sheer magnitude of the investment signals SpaceX's ambitious plans for AI computing capabilities. This financing structure through debt rather than equity allows SpaceX to maintain its ownership structure while accessing substantial capital for infrastructure expansion. The focus on GPU procurement specifically indicates plans for large-scale AI training and inference capabilities, as GPUs have become the essential hardware for modern artificial intelligence workloads. The timing of this investment aligns with broader industry trends showing unprecedented demand for AI computing resources. Major technology companies have been racing to secure GPU supplies, with manufacturers struggling to keep pace with demand. SpaceX's ability to secure financing of this magnitude demonstrates both the company's strong credit position and lenders' confidence in the strategic value of AI infrastructure. For SpaceX, which has traditionally focused on aerospace and satellite communications through its Starlink division, this represents a notable expansion of technical capabilities. The scale of GPU infrastructure being contemplated could support various applications, from enhancing autonomous systems in spacecraft to processing vast amounts of satellite imagery and data from Starlink's growing constellation. SpaceX's $40 billion debt financing for GPU infrastructure marks a pivotal moment in the convergence of aerospace and artificial intelligence technologies. While many questions remain about the specific applications and deployment timeline, the scale of this investment underscores how AI computing capabilities have become critical infrastructure across industries. As details emerge about how SpaceX plans to utilize this massive GPU capacity, the move could signal new directions for the company beyond its traditional aerospace focus.
